analysis.one_liner: Replaces congressional elections with ranked choice voting and multi-member districts, and bans partisan gerrymandering.
analysis.headline: The Fair Representation Act, introduced March 20, 2024 with 8 cosponsors, was sent to two House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how Americans elect the House and Senate. Every congressional election would use ranked choice voting, so voters could rank candidates in order of preference. States with more than a few House seats would replace single-member districts with districts electing 3 to 5 representatives together, so the minority party in an area could still win seats. States would also have to redraw their congressional maps without favoring either political party, and could not redraw them mid-decade. The bill provides federal payments of $4 to $8 per registered voter to help states run the new elections.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters whose votes currently count for little—people in districts drawn to be safely Republican or safely Democratic, members of minority parties within a state, and independent or third-party candidates—would get congressional elections where more votes translate into seats. Taxpayers in less partisan areas would no longer be locked out of competitive representation.

how_it_helps.text: Every congressional election would use ranked choice voting: voters rank candidates, and the candidate with the fewest votes in each round is eliminated with those votes moving to the voter's next choice, so a winner must reach out beyond a narrow base.

States with six or more House seats would draw districts electing 3 to 5 representatives together, and states with five or fewer would elect all representatives statewide, using a form of proportional counting—so a party earning 30% of the vote could win roughly 30% of the seats instead of none.
States could not use congressional maps drawn to materially favor or disfavor either political party, and could not redraw maps again mid-decade except when a court requires it.

Redistricting would have to happen through a public process: hearings in different regions of the state, proposed maps posted online with data and mapping software the public can use, and a written evaluation of each plan released before any vote.
Each state would receive a federal payment of $4 to $8 per registered voter to cover the cost of new voting equipment, ballot design, voter education, and tabulation for ranked choice voting.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress whose seats were made safe by district lines, and the two major party organizations that control primaries and redistricting, would lose the assurance of re-election and map control. Federal taxpayers would fund the state implementation payments, and election offices would take on the work of reprogramming equipment and educating voters.

drawbacks.text: Multi-member and at-large districts can weaken the one-to-one relationship between a constituent and a single representative, and can dilute the voting strength of a geographically concentrated minority group; the bill itself acknowledges this by carving out an exception where a court finds multi-member districts would diminish the ability of voters protected by the Voting Rights Act to elect their candidates of choice.

Ranked choice voting is harder to understand and administer: ballots can be set aside when a voter skips or repeats rankings, and results may take longer to tabulate, which costs election offices and can erode confidence during delays.

The implementation is funded by federal taxpayers, with payments authorized at $4 to $8 per registered voter nationally, and states would bear the operational burden of retraining staff and upgrading equipment even with the subsidy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the two mechanisms that insulate Congress from voters—partisan gerrymandering and winner-take-all single-seat districts—and the payoff for ordinary voters is substantial: more competitive elections, seats for minority-party voters, and a public, court-enforceable redistricting process. The costs are real but narrower: administrative complexity, slower or more confusing vote counting, weaker single-representative accountability, and a genuine risk to minority representation that the bill handles through a litigation-based exception rather than upfront design. A reasonable reading is that the benefits outweigh the costs, but the bill is an ambitious, constitutionally contested overhaul that Congress has never enacted at this scale.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees for the rest of the two-year Congress; neither ever held a hearing or vote, so the bill expired without ever being considered by the full House.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the Fair Representation Act on March 20, 2024, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Raskin, Blumenauer, Lee of California, Khanna, McGovern, and Peters.
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee and to the Committee on House Administration the day it was introduced; that referral was the only formal action of its entire life.
The bill never received a committee hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or a Senate companion's consideration before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress holding seats drawn to be safe for their party, and the party organizations that control primaries and redistricting in the states, are better off—no change was made to how congressional districts are drawn or how congressional elections are run, and incumbent-protecting maps remain in place.

for.name: Rep. Don Beyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Representation Act on March 20, 2024, laying out ranked choice voting, multi-member districts, and a ban on partisan gerrymandering for congressional elections.

for.name: Reps. Raskin, Blumenauer, Lee of California, Khanna, McGovern, and Peters
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, bringing total support to 9 House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: House leadership and committee chairs of the 118th Congress
against.role: Controlled the House floor and committee calendars
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration: the two committees of referral held no hearing or markup, and the bill was never brought to the House floor before the Congress ended.

against.name: Republican members of the House
against.what_they_did: None supported the bill; it drew no Republican cosponsors at any point in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: the sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored, while the Republican House majority never acted on it.

industries.note: Ranked choice voting, multi-member districts, and a ban on partisan-favoring maps all threaten the safe seats that most incumbents rely on. The bill never advanced in the chamber whose members it most directly affected.
Proportional multi-seat elections and nonpartisan redistricting criteria would end both parties' ability to lock in congressional majorities through map-drawing and gerrymandered primaries.

industries.industry: Election technology, ballot printing, and election administration vendors
industries.note: Federal payments of $4 to $8 per registered voter would fund new voting equipment, ballot design and printing, programming, and tabulation systems for ranked choice voting nationwide.
